textbookText: 2. Pharynx ( 3rd – 4th segment): Buccal chamber is followed by a wide, pear-shaped muscular structure called pharynx. Pharynx and buccal cavity are separated by a transverse constriction or groove. Pharynx extends from the middle of 3rd segment up to 4th segment Histologically, dorsal part or the roof of pharynx seems thicker and forms pharyngeal bulb. Similarly, its lateral wall is projected as horizontal fold or shelves; dividing the lumen (hollow cavity) incompletely into the dorsal salivary chamber and ventral conducting chamber. Pharyngeal bulb contains salivary glands composed of chromophil cells which secrete saliva and pour into salivary chamber. Saliva contains mucus and proteolytic enzymes. Mucus lubricates food and proteolytic enzymes digest protein. Ventral conducting chamber simply serves as the passage of food particles.

Figure 8.3.9 T. S. of body wall of earthworm through pharynx Pharynx remains connected with the body wall by muscular strands. Contraction and relaxation of these muscles help to compress and dilate the lumen of pharynx and this process facilitates in sucking and pumping of food particles. 3. Oesophagus (5th - 7th segment): Pharynx is followed posteriorly by a short narrow and thin-walled tubular structure, oesophagus. It extends from 5th to 7th segment. Oesophagus doesn’t contain any glands. Food passes downwards through it by peristalsis. 4. Gizzard (8th or 8th to 9th segment): Gizzard is a distinct, oval, hard, thick-walled and highly muscular organ. It is located in 8th or 8th to 9th segment and chiefly composed of thick layer of circular muscles. Lumen of gizzard is internally lined by cuticle. The function of gizzard is to grind or crush the food particles into fine state, thus acts as ‘grinding organ’.

Figure 8.3.10 T.S of earthworm through gizzard 5. Stomach (9th to 14th ): Gizzard leads into a short, narrow and thin-walled tube called stomach; extending from 9th to 14th segment with a sphincter at both ends. Its inner layer is highly vascular and glandular and thrown into internal transverse folds. Calciferous glands are found in the epithelial lining of stomach that produces Ca and CO2. These glands excrete excess Ca and CO3 ion in calcite form. 6. Intestine (15th onwards): Stomach is followed by a long, wide and thin-walled tubular structure called intestine. It extends from 15th segment up to the last segment. It appears beaded in structure because of circular constrictions corresponding to the septa. Intestine is divisible into 3 regions: pre-typhlosolar region, Typhlosolar region and Posttyphlosolar region. i. Pre-typhlosolar region: This region of intestine extends from 15th to 26th segment. Its inner wall is glandular, highly vascular and internally folded to form minute processes called villi. In the 26th segment, from the intestine arises a pair of lateral and upwardly directed conical outgrowths called intestinal caeca and each extends up to 23rd segment. These structures secrete amylase enzyme. They are also vascular and possess villi like processes. ii. Typhlosolar region: This is the second part of intestine which is characterized by the presence of a typhlosole. Typhlososle is a highly vascular, glandular and dorsal median longitudinal fold that extends from 27th segment onwards except last 25 segments. It is regarded as well-developed and largest villi. It has main role in the digestion and absorption of food.

iii. Post-typhlosolar region: Post typhlosolar region is the last part of the intestine, also called rectum. It is thinwalled vascular and comprises about last 25 segments. This region is devoid of typhlosole, villi and gland cells but its inner layer is longitudinally folded. It contains small pellets of mud as faeces.
Figure 8.3.12 T.S of earthworm through typhlosolar region 7. Anus:
Post typhlosolar region opens externally by a circular opening at the centre of last segment. Faecal matter (worm casting) is discharged through it.
